meta.title: A Conversation With Ken Griffin
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · AI and white-collar work · the GPU overcapacity question · Situational Awareness rescue · midterms and Trump scorecard · grow-your-way-out fiscal plan

snapshot: Ken Griffin on stage at the annual **Citadel Securities** conference, two weeks before the midterms, the same week semis logged their longest losing streak since the GFC.
AI now does in hours what Citadel's PhDs took 4-6 weeks to do; his Friday "depression" has turned into optimism about a **golden era for entrepreneurs**.
The AI sell-off is "people doing research": GPUs behave like airline seats — near-zero marginal cost — so if supply outruns demand, pricing goes into free fall, as with 2000-era fiber.
Calls hedge-fund deleveraging the excuse that "washes your hands of accountability" — it should be answer number 10, not number 1.
Citadel bought **Situational Awareness**'s portfolio in under 24 hours; he says that fund got caught in "three mid-size storms", including the Kimi announcement.
Expects Republicans to lose one or both houses; calls the Iran war's messaging poor, immigration enforcement "disgraceful" and tariffs "a disaster".

Fiscal fix is growth: productivity tech (AI, fission, fusion, batteries, robotics), education, Simpson-Bowles-style entitlement reform, green cards for top graduates. The bond market is speaking; Washington is "not yet" listening.

themes.title: AI fills in moats with bulldozers, but alpha still comes from people
themes.lead: Griffin says AI is game-changing for white-collar work, painful for incumbents and great for consumers and startups, while Citadel's edge stays human research.
bullets: Work that took Citadel's PhDs and masters 4-6 weeks now takes a few hours; the Stanford talk where he said so left him going home depressed one Friday.
Three emotions at once: the threat to white-collar jobs, competitive moats "filled in by bulldozers", and a golden era for new business formation.
English-to-German translators "probably have already lost" their jobs; the US needs reskilling "in a profound way" — there's talk but no action.
Startups hire people with "impaired pedigrees" and give them a new career lane; that's underrated.
Research is the core of the business, "almost like journalism"; AI sheds light on bits but the narrative is still assembled by a person.
Trading is the most automated, tech-forward part — monetizing research efficiently lets you run bigger positions.
Why it nets positive: "you and I would rather live right here in 2026 than in 1926."

quote.text: As a business owner, you're seeing your competitive modes be filled in by bulldozers.

themes.status: SEMIS' LONGEST LOSING STREAK SINCE THE GFC
themes.title: The AI trade grows discerning: GPU overcapacity, chip useful life and token bills
themes.lead: After two years of "buy them all", investors are asking how long choke-point margins last and whether GPU supply will outrun demand.
bullets: Old playbook: buy the hyperscalers, the chip companies, and Korean/Taiwanese/Japanese suppliers "I've never even heard of 5 years ago"; gatekeepers like Microsoft and AWS earn the rents.
Supply-constrained DRAM and MLCC margins are extreme; investors now look 2-3 years out to ask how long that lasts.
GPUs are like airline seats — very low marginal cost — so overcapacity sends pricing into free fall, as the 2000 fiber build-out did to telecom prices.
Useful life is the second worry: 5-6-year-old GPUs earn extraordinary pricing now, which "probably doesn't persist for another 5 or 6 years".
Corporate America is learning which work needs top-priced Anthropic/OpenAI models and which runs on open-source at a fraction of the cost — a lot of waste in some areas.
Host cites a WSJ report of ~$750B of planned spending in Anthropic's S-1; the open question is whether Anthropic becomes a must-have (e.g. cancer cures in pharma) with pricing power to match.
Bubbles: "almost certainly bubbles within this moment"; transformations come wrapped in bubbles (railroads, internet) and the survivors lead for decades — "I just wish I'd kept my Amazon stock".

quote.text: I think this market is actually experiencing people doing research.

themes.watch: The host cites Ray Dalio (bubble), Howard Marks ("bubble watch") and the BIS (dot-com echoes) on the other side; Griffin doesn't call the overall market a bubble.

themes.status: PORTFOLIO BOUGHT IN UNDER 24 HOURS — SUMMER 2026
themes.title: Situational Awareness rescue: three mid-size storms, and why deleveraging is excuse number 10
themes.lead: Griffin says Citadel bought the AI fund's portfolio on the theory that forced-sale prices snap back once the overhang clears, and "did okay".
bullets: "Everyone's favorite go-to answer when they're losing money is hedge funds are deleveraging" — he's seen the industry deleverage "to zero at least 10,000 times" in 10 years.
Makes it answer 10: first ask what Capital, Fidelity or Wellington figured out that Citadel didn't.
Situational Awareness needed to raise cash and protect a large year-to-date gain; it is still up significantly for the year.
Three storms: the Kimi announcement, chatter on foundation-model growth rates, and large pension plans reshaping portfolios — plus too much leverage at peak.
Fast money front-ran the expected selling, turning "a possibility into a crystallized reality" — a classic finance playbook.
Trade done in under 24 hours, risk managed over several days; precedents are Amaranth's energy book (~2006) and Sowood (2007).
Would be "a bit surprising" to see another like it soon; Citadel had its own moment in 2008 — had Morgan Stanley not landed its Japanese funding, "I don't think I'd be on stage today."

quote.text: The reason that people love that answer is it actually washes your hands of accountability.

themes.title: Griffin's Trump scorecard: Iran messaging, immigration and tariffs hurt; the border is a win
themes.lead: He expects Republicans to lose one or both houses and wants Trump to listen rather than double down.
bullets: Republicans "will almost certainly lose one or both" chambers; the House is in a really tough spot, the Senate will be close.
Backs Republicans but bundled for both parties: supported Rahm Emanuel for Chicago mayor and held an early Obama fundraiser; says a slight majority of Citadel staff are Democrats.
Iran war is very unpopular and badly explained, though a nuclear-free Iran is "of existential importance".
Treatment of illegal immigrants is "disgraceful"; employed long-term residents need a way to stay, even without citizenship.
Tariff battles with Canada and Europe "a disaster" — pro-inflation and supply-chain-severing; most people "don't want to be in factories making Nikes and t-shirts" (a comedian's line, he credits).
Reindustrialize with robotics instead — why he gave **$3B** to Carnegie Mellon, whose Miami campus he expects to transform the city.

Socialism: France spends 60% of GDP on government and its streets are in turmoil; Paris looked like Chicago in '21-'22. Names J.B. Pritzker, citing his failed Fair Tax amendment after rejecting a pensions-for-taxes deal Griffin offered.

quote.text: I hate to say it, but I've been right. It's been pro-inflation.

themes.watch: Griffin is a major Republican donor, was Illinois' largest taxpayer (his firm ~2% of state income tax) and has public feuds with Pritzker and New York's mayor.

themes.status: BOND MARKET SPEAKING — WASHINGTON "NOT YET" LISTENING
themes.title: Growth is the only way out of $40T of debt — and the bond market is already warning
themes.lead: Griffin's fiscal plan puts productivity first, then education, entitlement reform and skilled immigration; without it, inflation rises, the dollar weakens and living standards fall.
bullets: Pandemic spending as a share of GDP matched what the US spent to win World War II — "the cost of us sitting on our couches".
2018 tax cuts were "spot-on"; renewing them a year and change ago lacked fiscal space — Republicans' hands are "dirtier with the tax cuts" than with spending.
With **$40 trillion** of federal debt (he said "deficit"), crowding out is back: high 30-year yields and expensive mortgages.

Priority one, "grow the damn economy": data centers in America plus fusion, fission, batteries and robotics; push Europe to grow too — France's working-hour limits while the US funds its defense "doesn't work".
Two, fix schools: 53 Illinois schools had not one child at grade level; Eva Moskowitz's Success Academies works.

Three, a Simpson-Bowles-style up-down vote on entitlements, including working 1-3 more years before Social Security. Four, give foreign graduates (15-20% of elite schools) a green card with their degree.

quote.text: We're going to see higher inflation. We're going to see the dollar weaken, and we're going to see our standard of living fall.

takeaways.title: Stress-test AI hardware holdings for GPU overcapacity and shorter chip useful lives, not just demand
Rule out what other investors know before blaming a sell-off on hedge-fund deleveraging
Audit frontier-model spend and move commodity workloads to open-source models
Position for a likely split Congress after the Nov 2026 midterms
Read multi-decade-high long yields as the bond market's fiscal warning — a weaker dollar follows if ignored

hot_takes.take: In the last 10 years, I've seen the entire industry deleverage to zero at least 10,000 times.
GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run.

hot_takes.take: If you want to look at where socialism leads you to, look at France this last weekend.
If your expertise is in translation from English to German, for example, you probably have already lost your job.

claims.claim: Republicans will lose one or both houses of Congress in the midterms.
If GPU provisioning exceeds demand, marginal GPU pricing goes into free fall.
Extraordinary pricing on 5-6-year-old GPUs probably doesn't persist for another 5-6 years.
Another forced-portfolio event like Situational Awareness's would be surprising in the foreseeable future.
If Washington ignores the bond market, inflation rises, the dollar weakens and US living standards fall.
claims.condition: if fiscal house isn't put in order

other_news.title: Citadel's "center of gravity is somewhere over the middle of the Atlantic" between London, Miami and New York; 2,500 New York staff; teams kept in one location because "nothing beats a whiteboard and a good debate".
Miami: pro-business, safe streets, good schools, but housing costs and congested roads; credits the Cuban community for its anti-socialist ethos. Pittsburgh has ~100 robotics companies around CMU.
Sources referenced: a WSJ report on Anthropic's S-1, Ray Dalio, Howard Marks and the BIS (via the host), and Griffin's own Stanford talk.
